Source: https://butterfly-conservation.org/news-and-blog/science-news-accounting-for-species-phenology-to-estimate-population-trends-from-big
Title: Science News: Accounting for species’ phenology to estimate population trends from Big Butterfly Count data
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Emily Dennis explains how Butterfly Conservation accounts for species phenology when estimating population trends from the Big Butterfly Count.
Butterfly Conservation’s Big Butterfly Count is one of the world’s biggest nature-based citizen science projects, with over 125,000 people taking part in the UK this summer. The project has been hugely successful in engaging large numbers of observers and raising awareness of the state of the UK’s butterflies, but from a statistical perspective, analysing citizen-science data for biodiversity monitoring can present challenges, such as dealing with various forms of bias 1. In particular, the short three-week sampling period for Big Butterfly Count only captures a small window of species’ flight periods, thus between-year comparisons based on simple metrics are likely to be biased. A recent study2 led by Butterfly Conservation, in collaboration with the University of Kent and UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, has developed a new approach to account for this phenological bias, and thus enable the reporting of longer-term abundance trends from Big Butterfly Count data for the first time.
Butterfly abundance varies throughout the year as one or more generations of each species emerge and die off, and the timing (phenology) of emergences varies annually due to weather and climate. A previous study 3 based on Big Butterfly Count data from 2011-2014 showed that abundance change estimates for common butterfly species were comparable between Big Butterfly Count and the UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme (UKBMS) data, however it was also shown that the three-week sampling period rendered Big Butterfly Count “susceptible to bias caused by inter-annual phenological variation in the timing of species’ flight periods”. Thus, there may be the risk of a ‘groundhog effect’ – where a population decline may be falsely indicated by a species’ phenological shift in response to changing climate or other factors 4.

Published in the _Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics_, the new study used species’ flight curves estimated from standardised monitoring scheme data (UKBMS), to show that the proportion of the flight period captured by the Big Butterfly Count varies year-to-year for all species, but particularly for summer-flying univoltine (single generation) species, such as Marbled White and Ringlet. For example, the figure below shows how the Big Butterfly Count sampling period (shown in blue) captures different proportions of the Marbled White flight period in four example years, with the proportion varying from 0.12 (in 2011 and 2014) to 0.59 in 2012, when the species peaked comparatively later.
The study adapts a modelling approach that was developed for monitoring data (generalised abundance index 5), drawing upon phenology estimates from UKBMS data, to produce site-level (1km x 1km square) abundance estimates for Big Butterfly Count data that adjust for phenological bias. These phenology-corrected abundance estimates were then combined to produce relative abundance indices and trends for the UK from Big Butterfly Count data for 2011-2022 for 17 common and widespread species.
Comparison to UKBMS trends found that not accounting for phenology leads to biased trend estimates from the Big Butterfly Count data, particularly for the summer-flying univoltine species where the proportion of the flight period captured by the Big Butterfly Count was more variable. The Big Butterfly Count abundance trends were lower than UKBMS trends for 14 out of 17 species, which may be due to the two schemes sampling different habitats: UKBMS transect locations are biased towards sites that are managed for nature conservation, whereas Big Butterfly Count samples more urban habitats, in which butterfly populations have shown stronger declines than in rural areas 6. However, it is also noteworthy that the estimated trends were based on a relatively short period of 12 years which may be sensitive to start year 7 due to the high inter-annual variability in butterfly populations.

A simulation study showed that statistical power to detect trends in abundance was low when phenology adjustment was not applied. Meanwhile applying phenology adjustment resulted in generally unbiased trend estimates for a range of scenarios, such as varying species’ phenology and numbers of sites sampled, and demonstrated that current levels of Big Butterfly Count sampling were sufficient to detect a decrease of 25% over 12 years. The power to detect changes should increase with more years of data and the Big Butterfly Count therefore has the potential to reveal greater insights as longer-term trends become possible.
The new approach is already being implemented in the annual Big Butterfly Count results released by Butterfly Conservation, enabling phenologically-corrected long-term and year-to-year comparisons to be made. In summary, the new approach addresses the phenological bias that counts from snapshot citizen-science sampling are susceptible to, thus providing a basis for such data to contribute meaningfully to enhancing understanding of changes in butterfly populations, particularly in urban environments.
**Dr Emily Dennis**
Senior Ecological Statistician, Butterfly Conservation

**2. Dennis, E.B., Morgan, B.J.T., Harrower, C.A., Bourn, N.A.D & Fox, R.** (2024) Incorporating phenology to estimate species’ population trends from snapshot citizen-science data. _Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Environmental Statistics_doi:10.1007/s13253-024-00669-z

Title: Butterfly numbers increased this summer
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8
Show section menu
15 September 2023
Results of Butterfly Conservation’s Big Butterfly Count 2023 have been released today, revealing a better picture for butterflies than had been feared.
Video 3
Overall, participants of the Big Butterfly Count enjoyed seeing more butterflies this year than in the previous four summers. In total, over 1.5 million butterflies and day-flying moths were recorded from 14 July - 6 August. After an all-time low in 2022 of just nine individual butterflies spotted per Count, this year saw an increase to 12 butterflies recorded on average per Count.
However, this good news is in contrast with what the long-term trends are revealing. Released for the first time this year, these show that since the Big Butterfly Count started 13 years ago, many species have significantly decreased.
It is a further warning sign that nature everywhere is in crisis – butterflies, as well as forming a vital part of the food chain, are considered significant indicators of the health of the environment.
Following last summer’s heatwave and drought, scientists at Butterfly Conservation called on the public to help them understand the effect the extreme weather had on the UK’s butterflies. People responded in their thousands, with almost 95,000 citizen scientists taking part in this year’s Big Butterfly Count, conducting 136,719 15-minute Counts in gardens, parks, school grounds and the countryside.
Dr Zoe Randle, Senior Surveys Officer at Butterfly Conservation, said: _“It’s wonderful that so many people have been out enjoying spotting butterflies. We had huge support for Big Butterfly Count this year, and thanks to the many people who went out during those sunny intervals, we now know that the effects of last year’s drought were not as bad for butterflies as we had feared._
_“The mixed weather this year has helped as there has been an abundance of green food plants available for caterpillars, and plenty of nectar-rich flowers for adult butterflies. However, while the number of butterflies recorded this summer has been the highest since 2019, the longer-term trends show worrying declines for some of the UK’s most common butterfly species.”_

The most-seen species this year was the Red Admiral, with 248,077 recorded - an increase of 338% on last year’s Count and the first time the species, which is increasing in the UK as a result of climate change, has taken the top-spot.
Gatekeeper was next, with 222,896 sightings. This represents a 12% increase on last year and is a small, but welcome, boost for a species that has decreased by 28% since the Count began.
The Whites took the third and fourth spot, with 216,666 sightings of Large Whites and 190,506 of Small Whites, an 11% and 15% increase on 2022 respectively. Holly Blue had another good summer, with numbers up 66% on 2022, in keeping with its longer-term Big Butterfly Count trend of a 41% increase.
Species that saw a decline from last year include Ringlet, Common Blue and Speckled Wood, all of which also show long-term declines.
Although its numbers hardly changed compared to summer 2022, Green-veined White has the most severe Big Butterfly Count trend in the longer term, a decrease of 61%.
Dr Richard Fox, Head of Science at Butterfly Conservation, explained: _“One of the biggest threats butterflies in the UK face is habitat loss. While the weather certainly has an impact on numbers from year to year, butterflies, moths and many other species can generally cope with variable weather. What they can’t cope with is habitat destruction._
_“Butterflies need a place to live. If they can feed, breed and shelter, they can thrive. By creating a Wild Space in your outdoor area you can help to reverse the massive losses of wildlife-friendly habitat and start to turn around the fortunes of our declining butterflies."_

## Let's create more space for butterflies!
Anyone, anywhere, can create a Wild Space. Whether it’s leaving a patch of long grass in your garden or planting a small selection of nectar rich plants on a balcony, the opportunities are vast and everyone can make a difference.
Dr Richard Fox concluded: _“Nearly 137,000 Big Butterfly Counts were recorded this summer and if every single person who helped with the Count creates a Wild Space, we can build a UK-wide network of spaces for butterflies to feed, breed and shelter. By creating a Wild Space everyone can make a difference and help butterflies and moths thrive.”_
Butterfly Conservation has free resources and guidance on creating a Wild Space available, including accessible, tailored, simple advice for anyone to have a go.
**Find out more about Wild Spaces here**
_Next year’s Big Butterfly Count will take place from **Friday 12th July – Sunday 4th August 2024.**_

## Big Butterfly Count 2021 Wildlife Charity says we must act now if we are to save the UK's Butterflies and Moths
Wildlife charity warns that we must act now if we are to save the UK’s butterflies and moths for future generations.
Butterfly Conservation has today released data on the number of butterflies and day-flying moths counted across the UK in this year’s Big Butterfly Count, which ran from 16th July – 8th August.
Worryingly, the decline in the number of butterflies and moths across the UK is continuing, with the overall number of butterflies recorded per count at its lowest level since the Big Butterfly Count began 12 years ago.
Small Tortoiseshell
The nation’s love of butterflies isn’t diminishing. Despite the low butterfly numbers, and relatively poor weather, more butterfly counts were submitted than ever before. Over 150,000 counts were registered, representing more than 38,000 hours of butterfly counting in gardens, parks and the countryside.
Dr Zoë Randle, Senior Surveys Officer at Butterfly Conservation said: “This year’s results show that the average number of butterflies and moths per count is the lowest we’ve recorded so far. On average people counted nine butterflies or moths per count, which is down from 11 in 2020, and down again from 16 in 2019. More counts are undertaken and submitted year on year, but it seems that there are fewer butterflies and moths around to be counted.”
Some of the UK’s most-loved species including the Small Tortoiseshell and Peacock butterflies dropped in numbers this summer. The iconic Peacock butterfly suffered its lowest numbers since 2012. The Small Tortoiseshell, once a frequent visitor to gardens in the UK, had its third worst summer in the history of the Big Butterfly Count and shows a significant long-term decline in Britain.
Marbled White
I t wasn’t bad news for all species, with some, including the Marbled White and Ringlet, appearing to bounce back from their low numbers during last year’s Big Butterfly Count. However, scientists at Butterfly Conservation warn that last year’s unusually sunny spring allowed them to emerge earlier, and that 2021’s results are therefore more typical for these species.

## Big Butterfly Count 2021 Wildlife Charity says we must act now if we are to save the UK's Butterflies and Moths
This year’s weather has had a significant impact on butterfly and moth species, and with more climate change related extreme weather events likely, the impact on some of the UK’s most loved insects could be devastating.
Dr Randle explains: “Some of the UK’s butterflies have more than one generation per year, meaning we would see adult butterflies in spring and summer. The majority of these double-brooded species experienced their worst year since the start of the Big Butterfly Count in 2010. Weather changes are likely to be the cause of this. March 2021 was warmer than average which would have stimulated butterfly activity. However, May was very wet which will have hampered butterfly feeding and breeding. These combined weather effects are likely to have reduced the spring generation which has knock-on effects for the second generation in the summer.”
Butterflies and moths are important indicators of the health of the environment, and a decline in abundance is a serious cause for concern.
Butterfly Conservation has launched an ambitious strategy to help address the problems for butterflies and moths and be part of nature’s recovery.
Julie Williams, CEO of Butterfly Conservation, says: “The facts are clear. Nature is in crisis and we need urgent action, not just to prevent further species losses but to rebuild biodiversity.
“Since 1976, 76% of butterflies have declined in abundance or distribution, and the downward trend continues. We have come to accept that encounters with butterflies, moths and other wildlife are unusual, delightful but infrequent. It doesn’t have to be this way and through our new strategy Butterfly Conservation is pledging to halve the number of threatened butterfly and moth species in the UK, double our impact on landscape restoration, and galvanise thousands of people to create new wild spaces for nature.
“We can’t do this alone though and are urging people to join us to create a world where butterflies and moths thrive and can be enjoyed by everyone, everywhere.”
Butterfly Conservation has just unveiled an ambitious new strategy to combat the declines to butterfly and moth numbers that we've seen in the results of the Big Butterfly Count 2021. You can find out more about ithere.

Following last summer’s heatwave and drought, scientists at Butterfly Conservation called on the public to help them understand the effect the extreme weather had on the UK’s butterflies. However, while the number of butterflies recorded this summer has been the highest since 2019, the longer-term trends show worrying declines for some of the UK’s most common butterfly species.”_

The most-seen species this year was the Red Admiral, with 248,077 recorded - an increase of 338% on last year’s Count and the first time the species, which is increasing in the UK as a result of climate change, has taken the top-spot.
Gatekeeper was next, with 222,896 sightings. This represents a 12% increase on last year and is a small, but welcome, boost for a species that has decreased by 28% since the Count began.
The Whites took the third and fourth spot, with 216,666 sightings of Large Whites and 190,506 of Small Whites, an 11% and 15% increase on 2022 respectively. Holly Blue had another good summer, with numbers up 66% on 2022, in keeping with its longer-term Big Butterfly Count trend of a 41% increase.
Species that saw a decline from last year include Ringlet, Common Blue and Speckled Wood, all of which also show long-term declines.
Although its numbers hardly changed compared to summer 2022, Green-veined White has the most severe Big Butterfly Count trend in the longer term, a decrease of 61%.

While the weather certainly has an impact on numbers from year to year, butterflies, moths and many other species can generally cope with variable weather. What they can’t cope with is habitat destruction._
_“Butterflies need a place to live. If they can feed, breed and shelter, they can thrive. By creating a Wild Space in your outdoor area you can help to reverse the massive losses of wildlife-friendly habitat and start to turn around the fortunes of our declining butterflies."_

Anyone, anywhere, can create a Wild Space. Whether it’s leaving a patch of long grass in your garden or planting a small selection of nectar rich plants on a balcony, the opportunities are vast and everyone can make a difference.

Emily Dennis explains how Butterfly Conservation accounts for species phenology when estimating population trends from the Big Butterfly Count.
Butterfly Conservation’s Big Butterfly Count is one of the world’s biggest nature-based citizen science projects, with over 125,000 people taking part in the UK this summer. The project has been hugely successful in engaging large numbers of observers and raising awareness of the state of the UK’s butterflies, but from a statistical perspective, analysing citizen-science data for biodiversity monitoring can present challenges, such as dealing with various forms of bias 1. In particular, the short three-week sampling period for Big Butterfly Count only captures a small window of species’ flight periods, thus between-year comparisons based on simple metrics are likely to be biased. A recent study2 led by Butterfly Conservation, in collaboration with the University of Kent and UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, has developed a new approach to account for this phenological bias, and thus enable the reporting of longer-term abundance trends from Big Butterfly Count data for the first time.
Butterfly abundance varies throughout the year as one or more generations of each species emerge and die off, and the timing (phenology) of emergences varies annually due to weather and climate. A previous study 3 based on Big Butterfly Count data from 2011-2014 showed that abundance change estimates for common butterfly species were comparable between Big Butterfly Count and the UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme (UKBMS) data, however it was also shown that the three-week sampling period rendered Big Butterfly Count “susceptible to bias caused by inter-annual phenological variation in the timing of species’ flight periods”. Thus, there may be the risk of a ‘groundhog effect’ – where a population decline may be falsely indicated by a species’ phenological shift in response to changing climate or other factors 4.
texts.1:
Published in the _Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics_, the new study used species’ flight curves estimated from standardised monitoring scheme data (UKBMS), to show that the proportion of the flight period captured by the Big Butterfly Count varies year-to-year for all species, but particularly for summer-flying univoltine (single generation) species, such as Marbled White and Ringlet. For example, the figure below shows how the Big Butterfly Count sampling period (shown in blue) captures different proportions of the Marbled White flight period in four example years, with the proportion varying from 0.12 (in 2011 and 2014) to 0.59 in 2012, when the species peaked comparatively later.
The study adapts a modelling approach that was developed for monitoring data (generalised abundance index 5), drawing upon phenology estimates from UKBMS data, to produce site-level (1km x 1km square) abundance estimates for Big Butterfly Count data that adjust for phenological bias. These phenology-corrected abundance estimates were then combined to produce relative abundance indices and trends for the UK from Big Butterfly Count data for 2011-2022 for 17 common and widespread species.
Comparison to UKBMS trends found that not accounting for phenology leads to biased trend estimates from the Big Butterfly Count data, particularly for the summer-flying univoltine species where the proportion of the flight period captured by the Big Butterfly Count was more variable. The Big Butterfly Count abundance trends were lower than UKBMS trends for 14 out of 17 species, which may be due to the two schemes sampling different habitats: UKBMS transect locations are biased towards sites that are managed for nature conservation, whereas Big Butterfly Count samples more urban habitats, in which butterfly populations have shown stronger declines than in rural areas 6. However, it is also noteworthy that the estimated trends were based on a relatively short period of 12 years which may be sensitive to start year 7 due to the high inter-annual variability in butterfly populations.
texts.2:
A simulation study showed that statistical power to detect trends in abundance was low when phenology adjustment was not applied. Meanwhile applying phenology adjustment resulted in generally unbiased trend estimates for a range of scenarios, such as varying species’ phenology and numbers of sites sampled, and demonstrated that current levels of Big Butterfly Count sampling were sufficient to detect a decrease of 25% over 12 years. The power to detect changes should increase with more years of data and the Big Butterfly Count therefore has the potential to reveal greater insights as longer-term trends become possible.
The new approach is already being implemented in the annual Big Butterfly Count results released by Butterfly Conservation, enabling phenologically-corrected long-term and year-to-year comparisons to be made. In summary, the new approach addresses the phenological bias that counts from snapshot citizen-science sampling are susceptible to, thus providing a basis for such data to contribute meaningfully to enhancing understanding of changes in butterfly populations, particularly in urban environments.
**Dr Emily Dennis**
Senior Ecological Statistician, Butterfly Conservation

## Big Butterfly Count 2021 Wildlife Charity says we must act now if we are to save the UK's Butterflies and Moths
Wildlife charity warns that we must act now if we are to save the UK’s butterflies and moths for future generations.
Butterfly Conservation has today released data on the number of butterflies and day-flying moths counted across the UK in this year’s Big Butterfly Count, which ran from 16th July – 8th August.
Worryingly, the decline in the number of butterflies and moths across the UK is continuing, with the overall number of butterflies recorded per count at its lowest level since the Big Butterfly Count began 12 years ago.
Small Tortoiseshell
The nation’s love of butterflies isn’t diminishing. Despite the low butterfly numbers, and relatively poor weather, more butterfly counts were submitted than ever before. Over 150,000 counts were registered, representing more than 38,000 hours of butterfly counting in gardens, parks and the countryside.
Dr Zoë Randle, Senior Surveys Officer at Butterfly Conservation said: “This year’s results show that the average number of butterflies and moths per count is the lowest we’ve recorded so far. On average people counted nine butterflies or moths per count, which is down from 11 in 2020, and down again from 16 in 2019. More counts are undertaken and submitted year on year, but it seems that there are fewer butterflies and moths around to be counted.”
Some of the UK’s most-loved species including the Small Tortoiseshell and Peacock butterflies dropped in numbers this summer. The iconic Peacock butterfly suffered its lowest numbers since 2012. The Small Tortoiseshell, once a frequent visitor to gardens in the UK, had its third worst summer in the history of the Big Butterfly Count and shows a significant long-term decline in Britain.
Marbled White
I t wasn’t bad news for all species, with some, including the Marbled White and Ringlet, appearing to bounce back from their low numbers during last year’s Big Butterfly Count. However, scientists at Butterfly Conservation warn that last year’s unusually sunny spring allowed them to emerge earlier, and that 2021’s results are therefore more typical for these species.
texts.18:
## Big Butterfly Count 2021 Wildlife Charity says we must act now if we are to save the UK's Butterflies and Moths
This year’s weather has had a significant impact on butterfly and moth species, and with more climate change related extreme weather events likely, the impact on some of the UK’s most loved insects could be devastating.
Dr Randle explains: “Some of the UK’s butterflies have more than one generation per year, meaning we would see adult butterflies in spring and summer. The majority of these double-brooded species experienced their worst year since the start of the Big Butterfly Count in 2010. Weather changes are likely to be the cause of this. March 2021 was warmer than average which would have stimulated butterfly activity. However, May was very wet which will have hampered butterfly feeding and breeding. These combined weather effects are likely to have reduced the spring generation which has knock-on effects for the second generation in the summer.”
Butterflies and moths are important indicators of the health of the environment, and a decline in abundance is a serious cause for concern.
Butterfly Conservation has launched an ambitious strategy to help address the problems for butterflies and moths and be part of nature’s recovery.
Julie Williams, CEO of Butterfly Conservation, says: “The facts are clear. Nature is in crisis and we need urgent action, not just to prevent further species losses but to rebuild biodiversity.
“Since 1976, 76% of butterflies have declined in abundance or distribution, and the downward trend continues. We have come to accept that encounters with butterflies, moths and other wildlife are unusual, delightful but infrequent. It doesn’t have to be this way and through our new strategy Butterfly Conservation is pledging to halve the number of threatened butterfly and moth species in the UK, double our impact on landscape restoration, and galvanise thousands of people to create new wild spaces for nature.
“We can’t do this alone though and are urging people to join us to create a world where butterflies and moths thrive and can be enjoyed by everyone, everywhere.”
Butterfly Conservation has just unveiled an ambitious new strategy to combat the declines to butterfly and moth numbers that we've seen in the results of the Big Butterfly Count 2021. You can find out more about ithere.

Title: Science News: Accounting for species’ phenology to estimate population trends from Big Butterfly Count data
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Emily Dennis explains how Butterfly Conservation accounts for species phenology when estimating population trends from the Big Butterfly Count.
Butterfly Conservation’s Big Butterfly Count is one of the world’s biggest nature-based citizen science projects, with over 125,000 people taking part in the UK this summer. The project has been hugely successful in engaging large numbers of observers and raising awareness of the state of the UK’s butterflies, but from a statistical perspective, analysing citizen-science data for biodiversity monitoring can present challenges, such as dealing with various forms of bias 1. In particular, the short three-week sampling period for Big Butterfly Count only captures a small window of species’ flight periods, thus between-year comparisons based on simple metrics are likely to be biased. A recent study2 led by Butterfly Conservation, in collaboration with the University of Kent and UK Centre for Ecology & Hydrology, has developed a new approach to account for this phenological bias, and thus enable the reporting of longer-term abundance trends from Big Butterfly Count data for the first time.
Butterfly abundance varies throughout the year as one or more generations of each species emerge and die off, and the timing (phenology) of emergences varies annually due to weather and climate. A previous study 3 based on Big Butterfly Count data from 2011-2014 showed that abundance change estimates for common butterfly species were comparable between Big Butterfly Count and the UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme (UKBMS) data, however it was also shown that the three-week sampling period rendered Big Butterfly Count “susceptible to bias caused by inter-annual phenological variation in the timing of species’ flight periods”. Thus, there may be the risk of a ‘groundhog effect’ – where a population decline may be falsely indicated by a species’ phenological shift in response to changing climate or other factors 4.

Published in the _Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics_, the new study used species’ flight curves estimated from standardised monitoring scheme data (UKBMS), to show that the proportion of the flight period captured by the Big Butterfly Count varies year-to-year for all species, but particularly for summer-flying univoltine (single generation) species, such as Marbled White and Ringlet. For example, the figure below shows how the Big Butterfly Count sampling period (shown in blue) captures different proportions of the Marbled White flight period in four example years, with the proportion varying from 0.12 (in 2011 and 2014) to 0.59 in 2012, when the species peaked comparatively later.
The study adapts a modelling approach that was developed for monitoring data (generalised abundance index 5), drawing upon phenology estimates from UKBMS data, to produce site-level (1km x 1km square) abundance estimates for Big Butterfly Count data that adjust for phenological bias. These phenology-corrected abundance estimates were then combined to produce relative abundance indices and trends for the UK from Big Butterfly Count data for 2011-2022 for 17 common and widespread species.
Comparison to UKBMS trends found that not accounting for phenology leads to biased trend estimates from the Big Butterfly Count data, particularly for the summer-flying univoltine species where the proportion of the flight period captured by the Big Butterfly Count was more variable. The Big Butterfly Count abundance trends were lower than UKBMS trends for 14 out of 17 species, which may be due to the two schemes sampling different habitats: UKBMS transect locations are biased towards sites that are managed for nature conservation, whereas Big Butterfly Count samples more urban habitats, in which butterfly populations have shown stronger declines than in rural areas 6. However, it is also noteworthy that the estimated trends were based on a relatively short period of 12 years which may be sensitive to start year 7 due to the high inter-annual variability in butterfly populations.

A simulation study showed that statistical power to detect trends in abundance was low when phenology adjustment was not applied. Meanwhile applying phenology adjustment resulted in generally unbiased trend estimates for a range of scenarios, such as varying species’ phenology and numbers of sites sampled, and demonstrated that current levels of Big Butterfly Count sampling were sufficient to detect a decrease of 25% over 12 years. The power to detect changes should increase with more years of data and the Big Butterfly Count therefore has the potential to reveal greater insights as longer-term trends become possible.
The new approach is already being implemented in the annual Big Butterfly Count results released by Butterfly Conservation, enabling phenologically-corrected long-term and year-to-year comparisons to be made. In summary, the new approach addresses the phenological bias that counts from snapshot citizen-science sampling are susceptible to, thus providing a basis for such data to contribute meaningfully to enhancing understanding of changes in butterfly populations, particularly in urban environments.
**Dr Emily Dennis**
Senior Ecological Statistician, Butterfly Conservation

## Big Butterfly Count 2021 Wildlife Charity says we must act now if we are to save the UK's Butterflies and Moths
Wildlife charity warns that we must act now if we are to save the UK’s butterflies and moths for future generations.
Butterfly Conservation has today released data on the number of butterflies and day-flying moths counted across the UK in this year’s Big Butterfly Count, which ran from 16th July – 8th August.
Worryingly, the decline in the number of butterflies and moths across the UK is continuing, with the overall number of butterflies recorded per count at its lowest level since the Big Butterfly Count began 12 years ago.
Small Tortoiseshell
The nation’s love of butterflies isn’t diminishing. Despite the low butterfly numbers, and relatively poor weather, more butterfly counts were submitted than ever before. Over 150,000 counts were registered, representing more than 38,000 hours of butterfly counting in gardens, parks and the countryside.
Dr Zoë Randle, Senior Surveys Officer at Butterfly Conservation said: “This year’s results show that the average number of butterflies and moths per count is the lowest we’ve recorded so far. On average people counted nine butterflies or moths per count, which is down from 11 in 2020, and down again from 16 in 2019. More counts are undertaken and submitted year on year, but it seems that there are fewer butterflies and moths around to be counted.”
Some of the UK’s most-loved species including the Small Tortoiseshell and Peacock butterflies dropped in numbers this summer. The iconic Peacock butterfly suffered its lowest numbers since 2012. The Small Tortoiseshell, once a frequent visitor to gardens in the UK, had its third worst summer in the history of the Big Butterfly Count and shows a significant long-term decline in Britain.
Marbled White
I t wasn’t bad news for all species, with some, including the Marbled White and Ringlet, appearing to bounce back from their low numbers during last year’s Big Butterfly Count. However, scientists at Butterfly Conservation warn that last year’s unusually sunny spring allowed them to emerge earlier, and that 2021’s results are therefore more typical for these species.

## Big Butterfly Count 2021 Wildlife Charity says we must act now if we are to save the UK's Butterflies and Moths
This year’s weather has had a significant impact on butterfly and moth species, and with more climate change related extreme weather events likely, the impact on some of the UK’s most loved insects could be devastating.
Dr Randle explains: “Some of the UK’s butterflies have more than one generation per year, meaning we would see adult butterflies in spring and summer. The majority of these double-brooded species experienced their worst year since the start of the Big Butterfly Count in 2010. Weather changes are likely to be the cause of this. March 2021 was warmer than average which would have stimulated butterfly activity. However, May was very wet which will have hampered butterfly feeding and breeding. These combined weather effects are likely to have reduced the spring generation which has knock-on effects for the second generation in the summer.”
Butterflies and moths are important indicators of the health of the environment, and a decline in abundance is a serious cause for concern.
Butterfly Conservation has launched an ambitious strategy to help address the problems for butterflies and moths and be part of nature’s recovery.
Julie Williams, CEO of Butterfly Conservation, says: “The facts are clear. Nature is in crisis and we need urgent action, not just to prevent further species losses but to rebuild biodiversity.
“Since 1976, 76% of butterflies have declined in abundance or distribution, and the downward trend continues. We have come to accept that encounters with butterflies, moths and other wildlife are unusual, delightful but infrequent. It doesn’t have to be this way and through our new strategy Butterfly Conservation is pledging to halve the number of threatened butterfly and moth species in the UK, double our impact on landscape restoration, and galvanise thousands of people to create new wild spaces for nature.
“We can’t do this alone though and are urging people to join us to create a world where butterflies and moths thrive and can be enjoyed by everyone, everywhere.”
Butterfly Conservation has just unveiled an ambitious new strategy to combat the declines to butterfly and moth numbers that we've seen in the results of the Big Butterfly Count 2021. You can find out more about ithere.

decline in the UK since 1976, it has shown signs of recovery (+69%)  over the

Hills include a small colony near Knightford Bridge where over 10 sightings  
were recorded in May 2014 (TS, JT, TB).  However, Penny Hill Bank near  
Martley is the main str  onghold for this species with  over 50 sightings in 2014  
and 2015 (GL, JT, MW  i, PS, TB)./
Clouded Yellow  Colias croceus
A migrant which may breed after arrival in southern England to produce large  
numbers of north  -bound offspring. None were recorded locally, and there was  
only one transect si  ghting across the West Midlands in 2015.

## [PDF page 11]
Weather Summary for 2024
Overall, 2024 was a warm and unsettled year for the UK with  
exceptionally wet weather mid-May. The UK annual mean temperature  
was above the 1991-2020 long-term average; the fourth warmest year  
since 1991. Eight of the 12 months of the year saw temperatures above  
average, with February the second warmest on record, May the warmest,  
and December the fifth warmest. Despite several periods of exceptional  
rainfall, overall rainfall for the UK was around average. Winter was the  
eighth wettest on record, Spring was the sixth wettest and April was the  
sixth wettest. Sunshine was variable, but overall slightly below average.
January started mild, wet and unsettled, the middle of the month  
was cold but dry and the end of the month brought strong winds and rain,  
but also milder temperatures. Rainfall was close to average levels across  
the UK (97% of the long-term average) The the wet start and end to the  
month were compensated by the dry spell mid-month. Much of the UK  
experienced above-average sunshine hours (128% of the long-term  
average).
February was a mild but wet month with generally unsettled  
weather. A cold spell pushed into the north of the UK from the 6th  
onwards, with temperatures reaching 4.0 to 6.0°C below average in some  
areas of northern England on the 7th and 8th. Overall, the month was  
warmer and wetter than average. It was a fairly dull month for most of  
the UK (79% of the average sunshine hours).
March was unsettled, wet and dull. The month began colder than  
normal, however this was replaced with much milder weather for much of  
the rest of the month, although temperatures dipped again towards the  
end of the month. England recorded more than 150% of its long term  
average monthly rainfall and the mean temperature was 1.0°C above  
average. The month was dull, with the UK  recording just 95.2 hours of  
sunshine (87% of the long term average).

## [PDF page 11]
After a warmer than usual start to April, temperatures dropped,  
with the last two weeks of April cooler than average. It was a wet month,  
with northern England being particularly wet, recording 176% of the  
average April rainfall. April was generally quite dull, with the UK recording  
only 122.9 hours of sunshine, 79% of the average.
Rainfall in May was at times heavy but otherwise patchy and light,  
with some bright, sunny spells throughout the month. The UK experienced  
its warmest May on record. Although the first half of the month saw  
average rainfall, amounts increased for many by the end of the month,  
resulting in 155% of the average May rainfall.  Sunshine hours were  
slightly below average, with the UK  recording 83% of the average for  
May.

## [PDF page 10]
Dingy Skipper  Erynnis tages
The number of local sightings remains disappointingly low with only three  
sightings  in  2015  and  four  in  2014  both  at  the  Knapp  &  Papermill  (GL).  
However, this is a well  -camouflaged species that is easily mistaken for Burnet  
Companion (a common day  -flying moth), and it is probably under  -recorded.  
The last sightings at other locations were in 2011 at The Purlieu (NQ) and  
2010  at  Ballard’s  Land  (JT).  Although  this  species  has  undergone  a  19%  
decline in the UK since 1976, it has shown signs of recovery (+69%)  over the  
last decade due to conservation efforts.  Sightings just beyond the Malvern  
Hills include a small colony near Knightford Bridge where over 10 sightings  
were recorded in May 2014 (TS, JT, TB).  However, Penny Hill Bank near  
Martley is the main str  onghold for this species with  over 50 sightings in 2014  
and 2015 (GL, JT, MW  i, PS, TB)./
Clouded Yellow  Colias croceus
A migrant which may breed after arrival in southern England to produce large  
numbers of north  -bound offspring. None were recorded locally, and there was  
only one transect si  ghting across the West Midlands in 2015.  
None recorded locally between 2010 and 2012 but widely seen in 2013 from  
early August to late October.  In August and September 2014  there were two  
sightings at Knapp & Papermill (GL, HG), three sightings at Old Hills (NQ,  
MM) and one in a garden near Barnard’s Green (RC); and the last sighting  
was on 2 Nov at Blackmore Park near Wood Street (SR).

## [PDF page 10]
This hardy butterfly was common in the early part of the season. The first  
casual sightings were on 07 Mar at Brotheridge Green, Upper Colwall and  
Hanley Swan (DV, EW, SR). In addition to 116 transect records, there were  
83 casual sightings submitted as  part of the Citizen Science Project.  
The peak abundance of this early breeding species probably preceded the  
transect  recording  period,  but  the  systematic  transect  method  still  allows  
meaningful annual comparisons to be made for this long  -lived species. Seen  
on all transects but mostly at B  rotheridge Green (24) and Knapp & Papermill  
(18). Transect numbers were up by 29 %  in 2015 on top of a 28% increase in  
2014. Last seen at Hanley Castle on 05 Oct (PT), a little later than on 30 Sep  
at Old Hills in 2014 (MM).

## [PDF page 11]
Large White & Small White  Pieris brassicae & P.  rapae
2015 was a mixed year for these species. Their annual numbers fluctuate  
widely, partly due to the variation in the arrival of immigrants with peak counts  
in July. Transect records for Large White were up by 74% in 2015 following a  
decrease of 75% in 2014  . The 2015 big butterfly count showed a similar trend  
with a 46% increase this year compared with a 65% reduction last year.  
Transect records for Small White were, again, disappointing i.e.13% lower in  
2015 following an even larger decrease of 73% in 2014. However, the number  
(115) recorded at the new transect Hills Court Farm far exceeds any other  
site. The 2015 BBC showed a  3% decrease this year compared with a 60%  
decrease last year.  
Casual sightings include the first Large White on 06 Apr at Chase End Hill  
(WC) and the first Small White on 06 Apr at Hollybed Farm (MM).
Green-veined White  Pieris napi
Transect counts were down  -31% in 2015 compared with  -10% in 2014. The  
BBC shows an even larger reduction of 42% this year compared with a similar  
decrease of 47% last year. However, this is still a widespread resident with  
greatest numbers at Knapp & Pa  permill (178).  
There were 29 casual sightings  , the first on 06 Apr at Chase End Hill (WC).
Orange-tip  Anthocharis cardamines

Transect records show a slight decrease of 4% in 2015, but this follows an  
increase of 39% in 2014 recovering to the numbers last seen in 2011, after  
the wet Spring of 2012 and the cold Spring of 2013.  
Greatest numbers were Knapp & Papermill (63) and Castlemorton Common  
(46). There were 52 casual records, the first on 06 Apr at Malvern Link (MW).

(AB); two on 08 Jun Ivyscar Rock (HG) and Westminster Qua  rry (TT); one on  
11 Jun Gardiner’s Quarry; one on 16 Jun Queen’s Drive (TP); one on 20 Jun

## [PDF page 21]
This common species decreased by 15% in UK over the past decade, but  
was  stable  on  regional  transects,  continuing  its  run  of  good  years  locally.  
Counts were impressive - Hollybed Farm transect (1716), Knapp & Papermill  
(1070). The common  est butterfly was reflected in the most casual sightings  
including 114 on 12 Jul Guarlford Straight (SR) and 50 on 10 Jul Cother Wood  
(DT). Records for more common species at new transect Hills Court Farm  
often exceed all other  s and the Meadow Brown total of 4038 is no exc  eption.
Small Heath  Coenonympha pamphilus
A 21% decline in 2015  , following 23% decline between 2013 and 2014  , is  
worrying for this species. Further, local numbers plummeted in 2009 and 2011  
although  they  recovered  the  next  year,  even  in  the  wet  2012,  and  2013  
continued a good year. There was a 46% loss across the West Midlands in  
2015. Nationally its numbers have  increased by 18% over the last decade  
although it has undergone a long  -term decrease of 54% in the UK.

Weather Summary for 2024
Overall, 2024 was a warm and unsettled year for the UK with  
exceptionally wet weather mid-May. The UK annual mean temperature  
was above the 1991-2020 long-term average; the fourth warmest year  
since 1991. Eight of the 12 months of the year saw temperatures above  
average, with February the second warmest on record, May the warmest,  
and December the fifth warmest. Despite several periods of exceptional  
rainfall, overall rainfall for the UK was around average. Winter was the  
eighth wettest on record, Spring was the sixth wettest and April was the  
sixth wettest. Sunshine was variable, but overall slightly below average.
January started mild, wet and unsettled, the middle of the month  
was cold but dry and the end of the month brought strong winds and rain,  
but also milder temperatures. Rainfall was close to average levels across  
the UK (97% of the long-term average) The the wet start and end to the  
month were compensated by the dry spell mid-month. Much of the UK  
experienced above-average sunshine hours (128% of the long-term  
average).
February was a mild but wet month with generally unsettled  
weather. A cold spell pushed into the north of the UK from the 6th  
onwards, with temperatures reaching 4.0 to 6.0°C below average in some  
areas of northern England on the 7th and 8th. Overall, the month was  
warmer and wetter than average. It was a fairly dull month for most of  
the UK (79% of the average sunshine hours).
March was unsettled, wet and dull. The month began colder than  
normal, however this was replaced with much milder weather for much of  
the rest of the month, although temperatures dipped again towards the  
end of the month. England recorded more than 150% of its long term  
average monthly rainfall and the mean temperature was 1.0°C above  
average. The month was dull, with the UK  recording just 95.2 hours of  
sunshine (87% of the long term average).

## [PDF page 11]

with the last two weeks of April cooler than average. It was a wet month,  
with northern England being particularly wet, recording 176% of the  
average April rainfall. April was generally quite dull, with the UK recording  
only 122.9 hours of sunshine, 79% of the average.
Rainfall in May was at times heavy but otherwise patchy and light,  
with some bright, sunny spells throughout the month. The UK experienced  
its warmest May on record. Although the first half of the month saw  
average rainfall, amounts increased for many by the end of the month,  
resulting in 155% of the average May rainfall.  Sunshine hours were  
slightly below average, with the UK  recording 83% of the average for  
May.

## [PDF page 6]
Introduction
This report is compiled from a combination of transect and casual records.  
Fourteen transects are walked by volunteers on a weekly basis from April to  
September  and  counts  are  submitted  to  UK  Butterfly  Monitoring  Scheme  
(UKBMS).  Local  transect  counts  are  analysed  to  give  an  overview  of  the  
abundance  of  local  butterfly  species.  Local  abundancies  are  compared  
against regional counts from West Midlands Butterfly Conservation (WMBC)  
in 2018 and national UKBMS records as reported for 2014 (the latest report  
available) (Brereton et al. 2014).  Quoted short-term and long-term trends for  
the  UK  are  from  2005-2014  and  1976-2014,  respectively,  unless  stated  
otherwise. Butterfly Conservation’s 2018 Big Butterfly Count is also used for  
comparison.  
In addition to the transect records, more than 6500 butterfly and over 1600  
day-moth casual sightings  with  grid references were submitted to Malvern  
Butterfly  Group  (MBG).  Contributors  are  acknowledged  at  the  end  of  this  
report, although notable records are linked to the observer’s initials given to  
authorise species records. Details of site locations are also given at the end.  
Two new transect routes were introduced in 2017 and one further route in  
2018. Pinnacle Hill is one the best sites for Small Heath, Green Hairstreak  
and many common species. Poolbrook Common is the nearest site to Great  
Malvern and records high numbers of Small / Essex Skippers, Marbled White,  
Common Blue and some day-moths, especially Six-spot Burnet. Swinyard Hill  
transect  monitors  the  butterflies  further  south,  especially,  Silver-washed  
Fritillary around Hangman’s Hill.  
Butterfly Conservation produced an important report called “The State of the  
UK’s Butterflies 2015” with the headline “40 year slump for UK Butterflies”.  

## [PDF page 6]
More  than three  quarters  of UK’s butterfly species have  declined in  either  
abundance or occurrence (or both) in the last 40 years with some common  
species  suffering  significant  slumps.  Following  this  report,  local  species  
declined by 2% in abundance in 2015 and by 28% in 2016. However, numbers  
improved by over 70% during 2017 with similar numbers in 2018.  
In previous  years, nine transects were used to determine the  changes in  
annual  abundance  of  butterflies.  Overall,  based  on  the  average  adjusted  
transect total on nine sites, butterfly numbers in 2018 (1866) are the second  
highest  since  2011  compared  with  the  highest  in  2017  (1992)  and  2016  
(1137), 2015 (1583), 2014 (1618), 2013 (1557), 2012 (941) and 2011 (1269).  
However,  using  records  collected  from  13  local  transect  sites  (except  the  
newest Swinyard Hill), the average adjusted transect total in 2018 (2144) is  
also  the  second  highest  since  2017  (2275).  Interestingly,  both  measures  
suggest a decline of 6% since 2017.
4

## [PDF page 7]
Flight Times (taken from local records over recent years)
5

## [PDF page 8]
Overview of the local butterfly year
Population trends…  The slight decline in butterfly numbers on our transect  
sites  this  year  is  inevitably  subject  to  some  margin  of  error  and  is  not  
significant. In contrast, it is remarkable that butterfly numbers in 2017 and  
2018 are the highest since before 2011 (reliable figures are difficult to access  
and compare before this date). The populations of most of our common and  
less common species have increased  in 2018 compared with the average  
between 2011 and 2017. Not surprisingly, Meadow Brown is the commonest  
species (over 30% of the total count); while Ringlet remains second (over 10%  
total count). Notably, Small White have recovered numbers following several  
years of a worrying decline, to take over third position (8% total count), while  
Common  Blue  are  the  highest  in  recent  years  (fourth  position,  7.4%  total  
count). Marbled White has reached record levels in four continuous years (fifth  
position, 7.0%) and, for the first time is more common than Gatekeeper (sixth  
position, 6.6%) that suffered a decline this year but still not as bad as in 2016.  
The second generation of Brown Argus are now widespread and almost twice  
the number of Peacock, once very common and making a slight recovery in  
2018. Orange-tip numbers are possibly the lowest ever recorded, while Red  
Admiral  are  the  second  lowest  since  2011.  Small  Tortoiseshell  numbers  
changed little this year but are worryingly low compared with 2014.  
Three species  dominate the  higher slopes  of the  Malverns: Grayling, the  
rarest  species,  has  maintained  numbers  similar  to  last  year  but  is  still  
restricted to the eastern slopes of North Hill; Small Heath numbers are the  
highest since before 2011 and Small Copper numbers are the second highest  
since 2011.  
Transect counts for the less common species are not always reliable and  

## [PDF page 8]
depend  on  timed  counts  and,  to  some  extent,  on  casual  records.  Green  
Hairstreak and White-letter Hairstreak are low in numbers and do not seem to  
show a significant change in recent years; while Purple Hairstreak are lower  
on transect counts but, typically, higher in casual records. It is now arguable  
whether  Brown  Argus  should  be  considered  a  less  common  species  as  
numbers across all 14 transects are higher this year than 14 other species.  
Silver-washed  Fritillary  numbers  have  decreased  this  year  on  13  transect  
sites  but  show  an increase  when  the  new  Swinyard  transect  is  included.  
Rigorous  timed  counts  show  Grayling maintained  its highest  population  in  
2017 and 2018 for several years but it has failed to migrate to new sites.  
Annual numbers of migrant species fluctuate more widely than do residents  
due to more influencing factors over a larger geographic area. Although long-  
term  trends  for  migrants  are  encouraging,  the  short-term  trends  indicate  
significant declines in the UK. Local migrants had a disappointing year. Red  
Admiral declined to one of the lowest numbers in recent years following record
6

Source: https://butterfly-conservation.org/sites/default/files/2025-08/2016%20-BUTTERFLIES%20AROUND%20THE%20MALVERNS-REPORT-FINAL.pdf
Title: PDF document
Chunks: 29,30,31,32,42,43,44,45,46
## [PDF page 15]
There were 42% fewer transect records at only three sites in 2016 and 51%  
decrease over the past six years. Only one was recorded in the first brood at  
Melrose Farm Meadows. The second brood is typically more abundant and  
five were seen at North Hill and one at Old Hills. In 2015 five were seen at  
Brotheridge Green, five in Knapp & Papermill, two on Castlemorton Common,  
one  at Hollybed Farm, and two  at St. Wulstan’s NR.  There were only two  
casual sightings in 2016 both at Hills Court Farm  (MM), whereas in 2015 this  
site recorded 12 transect  records. It has a 25% long term decline in the UK.
Common Blue  Polyommatus icarus
Annual counts vary widely, in part depending on parasitism,  so perhaps it is  
no surprise to see a  huge decline of 85% in 2016 following the staggering  
increases of 141% in 2015  and 148% in 2014  . However, this represents a  
decline of 69  % in the past six years.  This may be linked to a  falling trend in a  
parasite-host cycle that peaked circa 2010  and 2015. The  WMBC awarded  
this species best performance for reaching a  five-year high in 2015  across  
West Midlands. However, the BBC showed declines of 55% in 2016 and 12%  
in 2015.  
Transect numbers were less than 20 at all sites except Knapp & Papermill  
(87). Nearby Hills Court Farm recorded 154 compared with an astounding 903
15

## [PDF page 16]
in 2015. This species is fairly colonial but variation could also be linked to  
localised  differences  in  the  parasite’s  timing.  Casual  sightings  (152)  were  
widespread across the eastern side of the Hills but notable records include  
105 at Poolbrook Common (AU) during six counts in August.
Holly Blue  Celastrina argiolus
Like the Common Blue, numbers are subject to annual fluctuations due to its  
complex  ecology,  particularly  with  two  species  of  parasitic  wasp  (braconid  
Cotesia inducta  & ichneumon Listrodomus nycthemerus  ) which tend to cause  
numbers  to  fluctuate  in  a  five  year  cycle.  However,  the  Holly  Blue  is  less  
colonial and typically widespread in low numbers.  Sightings in 2016 are similar  
to 2015 when there was an  increase of 63% compared with a fall of 28% in  
2014.  An  underlying  61%  decline  is  suggested  for  the  UK  over  the  last  
decade, making it difficult to find locally in poor years like 2014.  The highest  
transect count in 2016 was North Hill (21  ) and Old Hills (11) while other sites  
each  recorded  less  than  five  .  Casual  sightings  (64)  of  both  broods  were  
widespread in local gardens and around the Hills.
White Admiral  Limenitis camilla

## [PDF page 16]
This impressive canopy  -dweller was seen in similar numbers as last year,  
although  still  in  low  numbers  at  expected  locations.  White  Admirals  were  
patrolling woodland rides and edges, resting on the upper branches of large  
trees  and swooping  down  to visit  honeysuckle  – the caterpillar  food  plant.  
Seen  on  transects  at  Old  Hills  (  10)  and  Knapp  &  Papermill  (  1).  Casual  
sightings  include  Langdale  Wood  (SR  ,  MM),  and Swinyard  Hill  (RB). It  is  
probable  that  this  species  is  under-recorded  but  numbers  are  very  low,  
worrying for this vulnerable species with a 59% long-term decline in the UK.
Red Admiral  Vanessa atalanta
Numbers vary widely for this migrant species  : a decrease of  80% in 2013  , a  
huge increase of 344% in 2014, then a 40% decline in 2015. Numbers have  
recovered to some extent this year with transect records up by 28% in 2016  
and  6%  in  the  past  six  years.  The  BBC  show  similar  fluctuations:  43%  
increase in 2014, 28% down in 2015 and 70% up in 2016. WMBC awarded  
this  butterfly  the  most  improved  species  of  2016.  However,  a  long-term  
increase of 257% for the UK hides a 40% decline in the past 10 years.  
There was a record number  of 140 casual sightings  at regular intervals  from  
May  up to the middle of a relatively mild  November. One e  arlier sighting  in
16

## [PDF page 17]
February was seen nectaring on heather in Hall Green (SR). This individual  
may have survived the winter but would be unlikely to su  rvive to the end of  
spring – when mated migrants arrive  from the Continent  ready to lay eggs.  
Monday 31st October 2016.  ‘A very special day on the Hills with mild, sunny  
weather on the tops and glorious mist in the surrounding valleys. Sitting on a  
boulder just below t  he top of North Hill, I saw a large w  hite or yellow butterfly  
pass below but  , after chasing it around the eastern slopes  , I could not decide  
if it was a Brimstone, Large White or a migrant Clouded Yellow. However, Liz  
and I then saw at least four Red Admiral  – two pairs spiralling above the top  
and then separating  – presumably males c  ompeting for territory. Four more  
seen on Table Hill, one on Sugar Loaf, two on Worcestershire Beacon and  
one on Summer Hill  – and no doubt on every summit along the Malvern Ridge.  
But where are the females? I guess they had the good sense to migrate to the  
southern  Continent  to  e  njoy  the  sun,  the  nectar  and  the  mating.  These  
individuals may yet migrate but if they stay it is unlikely any will  survive to  
breed in the spring’  (MM, LL).
Painted Lady  Vanessa cardui
Only seen on five sites in 2016 following a rel  atively good year  in 2015 when  
seen on eight  out of  nine transects, but better than  only  three transects in  
2014. This represents a 23% decline in the past six years. However, 40 casual  
sightings between May and September from around the Malverns were more  
encouraging.  Like Red Admirals, they appear to migrate along the hilltops.  
The last record  in 2016 was 15-Sep at Upper Colwall (DT) while in  2015 it was  
01-Nov on the top of Sugarloaf (368m) during unusuall  y mild conditions 20  oC  
(MM).

## [PDF page 21]
were  seen  further  south  in  Firs  Valley,  Wide  Valley  and  Rushy  Valley  and  
further north on End Hill. In 2014 one was seen on Sugar Loaf and on  e on  
End Hill.
21

## [PDF page 22]
During May  2015 there were several carefully managed search  es for larvae  
(NQ, SR, MM, LL).  One was seen on Grayling Ridge and five around Chat  
Valley. None were found during one search in 2016  (MM, LL). In the past two  
years, adult pairs were seen courting,  mating  and  laying eggs on Grayling  
Ridge, Chat Valley and DeWalden  Loop. Several Grayling were seen taking  
nectar  in Chat Valley  and DWL.  The North Hill transect was set up to help  
monitor the Grayling population in the nearby quarries and the eastern tracks  
and slopes of North Hill. Grayling are sometimes seen on the upper and lower  
sections of the zigzag path but none  have been seen in the quarries or on the  
mid-section  of  the  zig-zag  path  in  recent  years.  Three  butterfly  walks  with  
WMBC,  MHC  and  MWT  in  July  allowed  nearly  30  volunteers  to  visit  the  
Grayling sites  .  
Grayling is a UK Biodiversity Action Plan Priority Species. WMBC and MBG  
are  working  closely  with  MHC  to  monitor  this  species  and  to  plan  the  
management of their habitat.  MHC continue to manage the habitat and restore  
acid  grasslands  containing  finer  grasses  to  encourage  the  Grayling  to  
recolonise suitable areas. MHC regularly organise  contract work and  work  
parties with a large group of enthusiastic volunteers to remove scrub  in the  
most  sensitive  areas,  especially  GR,  IS  R,  CV,  and  DWL  . WMBC  has  
successfully applied for limited funding  from Malvern AONB  to link and extend
22

## [PDF page 23]
the existing sites in 2017.  
Further information and analysis of data is available in the ‘  Report on the  
Population  &  Distribution  of  the  Malvern  Grayling  in  July  & August  2016  ’  
submitted by MM to MHC in September 2016  .
Gatekeeper  Pyronia tithonus
This common and widespread butterfly is subject to a 41% long  -term decline  
in the UK. In a poor year for most common species, the Gatekeeper competes  
with the Peacock for the lowest records in recent history. It  has consistently  
declined  each year since 2011 including  by 44% in 2016 and by 39% in the  
past six years  . However,  the highest transect counts include  Old Hills (273) &  
Hills  Court  Farm  (158). T  here  were  329  casual  sightings  from  around  the  
region, notably 50 on 27  -Jul at Poolbrook Common (AU), an  d 60 on 31  -Jul at  
Castlemorton Common (DT)
Meadow Brown  Maniola jurtina
This common species  has locally  decreased by 16% in the past six years  
and by 15% in UK over the past decade. Counts  are consistently high for the  
commonest butterfly  , particularly Hills Court  Farm transect (  1613), Hollybed  
Farm (1077) and  Knapp & Papermill (  811). Casual sightings  (1037) include  
62 on 07-Jul Guarlford Straight (SR)  , and 144 on 09  -Aug Poolbrook Common  
(AU).
Small Heath  Coenonympha pamphilus

## [PDF page 23]
Continual declines of 22% in 2016, 21% decline in 2015, and 23% in 2014,  
are worrying for this species. Over the past six years, it has declined by 37%.  
Furthermore, the occurrence of this species is declining,  and transect sites  
are restricted to the slopes of North Hill (76) and West Malvern (18) with only  
6 recorded at the lower site of Brotheridge Green. Nationally its numbers have  
increased by 18% over the last decade although it has undergone a long  -term  
decrease of 54% in the UK.  All casual sightings (128) are restricted the upper  
slopes and quarries between British Camp an  d North Hill  – notably 54 on 06  -  
Jun at British Camp (AB)  - with no recent sightings south of Hangman’s Hill  .  
The preference for the higher slopes can be explained to some extent  by the  
abundance of its  larval foodplants, especially  Sheep’s Fescue. However, this  
does not fully explain its apparent movement  northwards along the ridge and  
from lower sites over recent years.  Two broods are typical  but may overlap  
due to some caterpillars developing at different rates or even going into early
23

## [PDF page 24]
hibernation.
Ringlet  Aphantopus hyperantus
Ringlets  tolerate  humid  and  wet  s  ummers  and  will  fly  in  dull,  damp  
conditions. This summer was less sunny but drier than  usual. Local transects  
were 12% down in 2016 and 15%  down over the past six years  , although the  
Big Butterfly Count showed a  32% increase in 2016. Furthermore, it has a  
381% long-term increase in UK and a 72% increase over the last decade.  
Highest transect records include Old Hills (394) and Knapp & Papermill (185).  
Casual sightings (289) were widespread with notable records of 55 on 06-Jul  
at Neve’s Meadow (DT), 40 on 06-Jul at the Purlieu (DT) and 29 on 07-Jul at  
Guarlford Straight (SR).
Day-flying moths
Day-flying  moths  are  under  -recorded  locally  and  this  limited  selection  
pertains mostly to  437 incidental sightings by butterfly recorders  and includes  
some night-flying moths that can be seen during the day  (AU, AB, CG, DT,  
HG, JB, JL, LL, MM, MR, PG, PT, SR, SH, TD, TS).
Drab  Looper  Minoa  murinata  . There  were  only  three  sightings  (photos  
taken) of this rare species on 8-Jun (2) & 11-Jun (1) at Gullet Quarry (MM).  
This compares with 10 sightings at this location in 2015 (SR, MM). Two were  
also seen in 2015 on 26-May near the summit of Chase End Hill (TS). These  
are the first sightings since May and early June 2011 at Chase End Hill,  
Gullet Quarry and News Wood (SR). This moth is scarce and found only in  
sunny woodland clearings in isolated areas of southern England and the  
Welsh borders.

## The Big Bufferfly Count Results for Norfolk
Thank to all those who took part in the Big Butterfly count for 2025. As you can see from the results number of counts and the number of butterflies recorded have increased.
Here are the 2025 data for Norfolk, with 2024 numbers in brackets.
Total number of butterflies: 54849 (29470)
Percentage change from 2024 to 2025: 86%
Total number of counts: 4225 (3908)
Average number of butterflies per count:12.98 (7.54)

## Members' Afternoon and Photographic Competition
Our member afternoon and photographic competition takes place on Saturday 11th October at Hethersett Village Hall, Back Lane Hethersett between 2:00pn and 4:30pm.
Our guest speaker this year is Mike Slater who has been a member of Butterfly Conservation for over 50 years and is the Volunteer Conservation Officer for the Warwickshire branch.
During the midway break you will have the opportunity to vote on the entries to the Photographic Competition.
Further details can be found in the Spring Newsletter and on the events page at here
* * *

## **Field Trip to Middle Harling 23 July**
On a very damp and dismal morning 9 BC members met to walk the Middle Harling transect. Andy and Claire, who regularly walk this transect, led the way and despite the poor conditions butterflies were seen! After several weeks of dry, hot weather the recent rain had encouraged a profusion of wild flowers and the Heath looked wonderful.
A total of 64 butterflies was recorded and species included Small and Large Skippers, Small, Large and Green-veined White, Common Blue, Red Admiral, Comma, Speckled Wood, Meadow Brown, Ringlet, Small Heath and Gatekeepers which were, by far, the most numerous.
It was unanimously agreed that it had been a most enjoyable morning.
* * *

## Marsh Special Recognition Award


## We are pleased to tell you that Alan Dawson the transect Coordinator together with his late wife, Chris, has received a Marsh Special Recognition Award with Butterfly Conservation. The citation reads “ Your long-standing dedication and contributions to Butterfly Conservation, alongside your late wife, are exceptional and have been recognised by the judging panel as outstanding”.
* * *

## 21st April The Members newsletter
The Members newsletter should be dropping through your letter box shortly, containing butterfly survey results for 2024. Probably no surprise to any butterfly watcher is that the news is not great. Once common butterflies Peacock & Small Tortoiseshell had a particularly bad year, on the plus side Dark Green Fritillary and Green Hairstreak numbers bounced back.
* * *

## 20th April
At least 4 species of butterfly on the wing at NT Sheringham Park this Easter weekend. Frequent sightings of Orange Tip, as well as 2 Red Admirals, a single Brimstone and a late afternoon Comma
* * *

## 14th April
We have received a report one of Norfolk's most endangered species on the wing. Grizzled skipper as well as being rare is difficult to see. It's small, flies fast and very low. Keep you eyes peeled for movement close to the ground
* * *

## The Norfolk branch is now on Bluesky
We have added Bluesky to our social media options.
You can find us at @norfolkbutterflies.bsky.social. Please like and follow.
* * *

## Big Butterfly Count Norfolk 2024
We thank the 2329 people who took part in the Big Butterfly Count in Norfolk during the summer counting 27,885 butterflies and day-flying moths.
The results for our county make sobering reading. Numbers of butterflies per count were 7 compared to last year’s 14. Of the 20 species counted only Ringlet and Six-spot Burnet appeared to have fared well in this year compared to 2023, however, this was due to their peak flight periods coinciding with the count.
Gatekeeper was our number 1, jumping from 4 th place in 2023. Despite this its numbers were still down by over a quarter.
Our chart topper last year Peacock fell to number 5 with its numbers down by an average of 70% per count, Red Admiral at number 2 in 2023 slipped to number 6 with a 75% reduction.
The once common Small Tortoiseshell slipped out of the top 10 with only 0.08 butterflies per count, Norfolk is now below the national average for this species which in itself was the lowest since the count started 14 years ago.
We achieved good coverage for Norfolk, but there are a few gaps (see map). Can you help us fill these in 2025?
**The Big Butterfly Count runs from Friday 18th July – Sunday 10th August. Please put a note in your diary.**
Let’s hope for better results in 2025.

and I then saw at least four Red Admiral  – two pairs spiralling above the top  
and then separating  – presumably males c  ompeting for territory. Four more  
seen on Table Hill, one on Sugar Loaf, two on Worcestershire Beacon and  
one on Summer Hill  – and no doubt on every summit along the Malvern Ridge.  
But where are the females? I guess they had the good sense to migrate to the  
southern  Continent  to  e  njoy  the  sun,  the  nectar  and  the  mating.  These  
individuals may yet migrate but if they stay it is unlikely any will  survive to  
breed in the spring’  (MM, LL).
Painted Lady  Vanessa cardui
Only seen on five sites in 2016 following a rel  atively good year  in 2015 when  
seen on eight  out of  nine transects, but better than  only  three transects in  
2014. This represents a 23% decline in the past six years. However, 40 casual  
sightings between May and September from around the Malverns were more  
encouraging.  Like Red Admirals, they appear to migrate along the hilltops.  
The last record  in 2016 was 15-Sep at Upper Colwall (DT) while in  2015 it was  
01-Nov on the top of Sugarloaf (368m) during unusuall  y mild conditions 20  oC  
(MM).

During May  2015 there were several carefully managed search  es for larvae  
(NQ, SR, MM, LL).  One was seen on Grayling Ridge and five around Chat  
Valley. None were found during one search in 2016  (MM, LL). In the past two  
years, adult pairs were seen courting,  mating  and  laying eggs on Grayling  
Ridge, Chat Valley and DeWalden  Loop. Several Grayling were seen taking  
nectar  in Chat Valley  and DWL.  The North Hill transect was set up to help  
monitor the Grayling population in the nearby quarries and the eastern tracks  
and slopes of North Hill. Grayling are sometimes seen on the upper and lower  
sections of the zigzag path but none  have been seen in the quarries or on the  
mid-section  of  the  zig-zag  path  in  recent  years.  Three  butterfly  walks  with  
WMBC,  MHC  and  MWT  in  July  allowed  nearly  30  volunteers  to  visit  the  
Grayling sites  .  
Grayling is a UK Biodiversity Action Plan Priority Species. WMBC and MBG  
are  working  closely  with  MHC  to  monitor  this  species  and  to  plan  the  
management of their habitat.  MHC continue to manage the habitat and restore  
acid  grasslands  containing  finer  grasses  to  encourage  the  Grayling  to  
recolonise suitable areas. MHC regularly organise  contract work and  work  
parties with a large group of enthusiastic volunteers to remove scrub  in the  
most  sensitive  areas,  especially  GR,  IS  R,  CV,  and  DWL  . WMBC  has  
successfully applied for limited funding  from Malvern AONB  to link and extend

## [PDF page 23]
Continual declines of 22% in 2016, 21% decline in 2015, and 23% in 2014,  
are worrying for this species. Over the past six years, it has declined by 37%.  
Furthermore, the occurrence of this species is declining,  and transect sites  
are restricted to the slopes of North Hill (76) and West Malvern (18) with only  
6 recorded at the lower site of Brotheridge Green. Nationally its numbers have  
increased by 18% over the last decade although it has undergone a long  -term  
decrease of 54% in the UK.  All casual sightings (128) are restricted the upper  
slopes and quarries between British Camp an  d North Hill  – notably 54 on 06  -  
Jun at British Camp (AB)  - with no recent sightings south of Hangman’s Hill  .  
The preference for the higher slopes can be explained to some extent  by the  
abundance of its  larval foodplants, especially  Sheep’s Fescue. However, this  
does not fully explain its apparent movement  northwards along the ridge and  
from lower sites over recent years.  Two broods are typical  but may overlap  
due to some caterpillars developing at different rates or even going into early

Ringlet  Aphantopus hyperantus
Ringlets  tolerate  humid  and  wet  s  ummers  and  will  fly  in  dull,  damp  
conditions. This summer was less sunny but drier than  usual. Local transects  
were 12% down in 2016 and 15%  down over the past six years  , although the  
Big Butterfly Count showed a  32% increase in 2016. Furthermore, it has a

Day-flying moths
Day-flying  moths  are  under  -recorded  locally  and  this  limited  selection

Drab  Looper  Minoa  murinata  . There  were  only  three  sightings  (photos  
taken) of this rare species on 8-Jun (2) & 11-Jun (1) at Gullet Quarry (MM).  
This compares with 10 sightings at this location in 2015 (SR, MM). Two were  
also seen in 2015 on 26-May near the summit of Chase End Hill (TS). These  
are the first sightings since May and early June 2011 at Chase End Hill,  
Gullet Quarry and News Wood (SR). This moth is scarce and found only in  
sunny woodland clearings in isolated areas of southern England and the  
Welsh borders.

texts.6:
## [PDF page 6]
Introduction
This report is compiled from a combination of transect and casual records.  
Fourteen transects are walked by volunteers on a weekly basis from April to  
September  and  counts  are  submitted  to  UK  Butterfly  Monitoring  Scheme  
(UKBMS).  Local  transect  counts  are  analysed  to  give  an  overview  of  the  
abundance  of  local  butterfly  species.  Local  abundancies  are  compared  
against regional counts from West Midlands Butterfly Conservation (WMBC)  
in 2018 and national UKBMS records as reported for 2014 (the latest report  
available) (Brereton et al. 2014).  Quoted short-term and long-term trends for  
the  UK  are  from  2005-2014  and  1976-2014,  respectively,  unless  stated  
otherwise. Butterfly Conservation’s 2018 Big Butterfly Count is also used for  
comparison.  
In addition to the transect records, more than 6500 butterfly and over 1600  
day-moth casual sightings  with  grid references were submitted to Malvern  
Butterfly  Group  (MBG).  Contributors  are  acknowledged  at  the  end  of  this  
report, although notable records are linked to the observer’s initials given to  
authorise species records. Details of site locations are also given at the end.  
Two new transect routes were introduced in 2017 and one further route in  
2018. Pinnacle Hill is one the best sites for Small Heath, Green Hairstreak  
and many common species. Poolbrook Common is the nearest site to Great  
Malvern and records high numbers of Small / Essex Skippers, Marbled White,  
Common Blue and some day-moths, especially Six-spot Burnet. Swinyard Hill  
transect  monitors  the  butterflies  further  south,  especially,  Silver-washed  
Fritillary around Hangman’s Hill.  
Butterfly Conservation produced an important report called “The State of the  
UK’s Butterflies 2015” with the headline “40 year slump for UK Butterflies”.
texts.7:
## [PDF page 6]
More  than three  quarters  of UK’s butterfly species have  declined in  either  
abundance or occurrence (or both) in the last 40 years with some common  
species  suffering  significant  slumps.  Following  this  report,  local  species  
declined by 2% in abundance in 2015 and by 28% in 2016. However, numbers  
improved by over 70% during 2017 with similar numbers in 2018.  
In previous  years, nine transects were used to determine the  changes in  
annual  abundance  of  butterflies.  Overall,  based  on  the  average  adjusted  
transect total on nine sites, butterfly numbers in 2018 (1866) are the second  
highest  since  2011  compared  with  the  highest  in  2017  (1992)  and  2016  
(1137), 2015 (1583), 2014 (1618), 2013 (1557), 2012 (941) and 2011 (1269).  
However,  using  records  collected  from  13  local  transect  sites  (except  the  
newest Swinyard Hill), the average adjusted transect total in 2018 (2144) is  
also  the  second  highest  since  2017  (2275).  Interestingly,  both  measures  
suggest a decline of 6% since 2017.
